note: Claim is definitively REFUTED by two major lines of prior work: (1) Colledanchise & Ogren (2017 IEEE T-RO and 2018 CRC book, Chapter 5: 'Analysis of Efficiency, Safety, and Robustness') explicitly formalizes subtree-level contracts and structural composition. Definition 5.5 defines Finite Time Successful (FTS) subtree contracts with regions of attraction (preconditions) and success sets (postconditions/return status); Lemma 5.2 (Sequence), Lemma 5.3 (Fallback), and Lemma 5.5 (Safety) prove that if subtrees satisfy contracts in isolation and interface conditions match (e.g. S1 = R02 U S2), the composed tree is guaranteed to satisfy the composite contract. Section 5.4.3 proves safety and FTS for a complex humanoid robot BT by composing isolated subtree contracts. (2) Oliver Biggar & Mohammad Zamani (IEEE RA-L 2020, 'A Framework for Formal Verification of Behavior Trees With Linear Temporal Logic') developed an assume-guarantee refinement framework for discrete LTL verification: subtrees have contract triples (succ, fail, guar), subtrees are verified in isolation against local contracts/environments, and a substitution theorem guarantees whole-tree specifications hold. In fact, Biggar's code is in this very repo at REPRODUCIBILITY/OTHER_TOOLS/biggar2020Framework/. Other checks: arXiv 2012.01648 does not use BTs; BT2Fiacre (2502.11904), MoVe4BT, and SETTA 2023 are all monolithic compilations (Tina/PAT).

note: REFUTED on both literature and analytical grounds: (1) Literature: Colledanchise & Ogren (2017/2018) contains no multi-agent chapters; Biggar & Zamani (2020) parallel composition requires disjoint variables; no prior work does per-agent A/G or cutoff theorems on BTs. (2) Analytical failure on the ring benchmark: Progress on an N-robot ring with N+1 positions is a global token-passing protocol (the single empty slot circulating). Robot i cannot move until i+1 moves, which needs i+2, forming an unbroken dependency cycle of length N. Proving liveness AG(AF(x_i = goal_i)) requires assuming no robot halts, which transitively depends on all N agents. Local contracts cannot break this cycle without a global invariant mentioning all N positions. (3) Empirical foundation collapsed: The 43-node ring does not have 2.1M reachable states—nuXmv print_reachable_states confirms exactly 23 reachable states. The 103s runtime is BDD CTL fixed-point overhead on coupled transitions, not state space explosion.

REFUTED: (1) The ring_7 reachable state space is NOT 2,097,152 states; nuXmv print_reachable_states proves it has exactly 23 reachable states (strictly deterministic token rotation of 3 steps per robot). (2) The 0.15s on FiveInRing.tree vs 103s on ring_7 is an apples-to-oranges artefact of gen_ring.py: FiveInRing.tree has an intentional deadlock where r4 parks at tick 0, so 8 of 10 CTL specs are FALSE and nuXmv exits in 0.15s on a 5-step counterexample lasso. In gen_ring.py, goal = (i+3)%npos eliminates deadlock, making all CTLSPECs TRUE. Proving AG AF true requires nuXmv to compute nested least/greatest BDD fixed points (check_invar takes 0.10s; check_ctlspec takes the remaining 103s). The cost is driven by nuXmv BDD variable ordering on monolithic CTL liveness, not by concurrent-agent state space size.

statement: Large reachable state spaces in BTs (3M-7.4M) do not bottleneck monolithic BDD model checking (verifying in 0.15s to 45s); verification bottlenecks in BTs are driven by cyclic BDD variable coupling in nested CTL fixpoints or massive transition constraints from continuous dynamics, creating a structural dilemma for compositional verification.
evidence: DrunkenDrone (3.06M reachable) verifies CTL in 0.15s; drone3 (7.43M reachable, diameter 950) verifies 5 INVARs and 1 CTL in 45s. In contrast, ring_7 has only 23 reachable states but takes 124s without dynamic BDD reordering due to cyclic variable coupling in CTL fixpoints. When reachable state spaces are large and regular, BDDs handle them efficiently; when monolithic model checking struggles, cyclic dependencies prevent local assume-guarantee contracts from breaking the cycle.

statement: No cutoff theorems or parameterized model checking results exist in the published Behavior Tree literature; extending classical cutoff results (Emerson & Namjoshi, German & Sistla) to multi-agent BTs is fundamentally obstructed because agent coordination in robotics relies on heterogeneous spatial destinations (goal_i != goal_j) and cyclic token dependencies, breaking permutation symmetry.
evidence: Survey of Colledanchise & Ogren (2017/2018), Biggar & Zamani (2020), MoVe4BT (2021), BT2Fiacre (2021), BT2BIP (2022), and BehaVerify (2022-2026) reveals zero cutoff theorems for BTs. Emerson & Namjoshi (1995) cutoffs require index-symmetric process topologies; FiveInRing and warehouse swarms break symmetry via distinct fixed destination coordinates, rendering standard cutoff reductions inapplicable.

statement: BT verification tools (BehaVerify, BT2Fiacre, BT2BIP, MoVe4BT, ArcadeBT) universally acknowledge in their limitations and future work that they are restricted to discrete or finite-domain state spaces, with explicit quotes admitting failures on continuous/real variables, dynamic modifications, and environment concurrency.

statement: No state-of-the-art closed-loop neural network verifier (CORA, JuliaReach, NNV, Verisig 2.0, POLAR) supports discrete execution structure, mode sequencing, or temporal logic over control flow (LTL/CTL) in the controller; all evaluate continuous reach-avoid or trajectory-level STL over a single monolithic feedback policy u = pi(x) or fixed mode plant.
evidence: ARCH-COMP AINNCS reports (2021-2025) show 100% of benchmarks (ACC, TORA, CartPole, Quadrotor, Airplane, Unicycle, NAV) feature a single feedforward policy without switching or hierarchical branching; JuliaReach ClosedLoopReachability.jl and NNV support hybrid automata plant dynamics but zero controller discrete state machines or behavior tree semantics (ticks, return status, Sequences, Fallbacks).

statement: Compiling Behavior Trees with continuous dynamics into Hybrid Automata for continuous verification by hybrid tools (Flow*, SpaceEx, CORA) causes an immediate flowpipe fragmentation explosion due to high-frequency discrete guard intersections at every BT tick.
evidence: In hybrid reachability tools, each discrete guard crossing splits or over-approximates continuous sets (zonotopes/Taylor models). A BT ticking at frequency f (e.g. 10 Hz) across branching condition nodes produces up to 2^(f*T) discrete branch intersections over time horizon T, exceeding the 10-20 mode-switch ceiling of modern flowpipe tools within seconds.

statement: Behavior Tree synthesis from formal specifications is split into two solved or unviable regimes: deterministic task planning is already solved by provably correct-by-construction BT Expansion (Colledanchise & Ogren 2019/2021), while LTL synthesis via MCTS/model checking (Synthesizer4BT) suffers from double exponential state explosion, has produced no available code (empty GitHub repository as of 2026), and provides no semantic advantage over standard reactive synthesis (GR(1)) to state machines.
evidence: Colledanchise & Ogren (2019/2021) algorithm synthesizes BTs from pre/post-conditions with formal convergence guarantees; Synthesizer4BT repo (FM4BT/Synthesizer4BT) contains 0 lines of code (only README saying 'The source code will be available later'); general LTL synthesis to trees is strictly harder than synthesis to Mealy machines because tree structural constraints restrict valid transition topologies without adding expressiveness.

statement: Runtime monitoring of Behavior Trees against temporal logic specifications is an already-solved problem with multiple existing implementations, including BehaVerify's own src/behaverify/monitor/ module (FMAS 2024), Hippo/BT2Fiacre, and ROS-based monitor frameworks.
evidence: Serbinowska, Potteiger, Tumlin, Johnson (FMAS 2024, arXiv:2411.14162) introduced contingency monitors for BTs (BTMs) and implemented Python and C runtime monitor generators (create_python_monitor.py, create_c_monitor.py) in BehaVerify; Felix et al. (arXiv:2502.11904) provides the Hippo runtime verification engine executing Fiacre-compiled BT models online; Colledanchise et al. (IROS 2021) formalized execution context for BT runtime verification.

statement: Falsification (black-box / optimization-based counterexample search via S-TaLiRo / Breach) can already be applied out-of-the-box to Behavior Trees wrapped as Python/C++ black-box controllers, while developing a dedicated 'white-box BT falsifier' is an open but uninteresting engineering direction dominated by optimization heuristics over discontinuous fitness landscapes.
evidence: S-TaLiRo and Breach require only a trajectory simulation oracle y = f(x_0, u(t)) and an STL specification phi; any executable BT (PyTrees/BehaviorTree.CPP) can be called directly without theoretical novelty. White-box falsification encounters step-discontinuities at condition guards where gradient falsification degrades to random/genetic search, offering minimal academic contribution over standard search-based software testing.

statement: Probabilistic and timed Behavior Tree verification are already solved via compilation to existing model checkers (PRISM, Storm, Tina/TTS, UPPAAL) with established literature dating back to 2018, leaving no foundational research gap.
evidence: Colledanchise & Ogren (2018 book Ch. 9) mapped stochastic BTs to DTMCs; multiple subsequent papers compile BTs to PRISM/Storm via JANI for PCTL/CSL verification; Felix et al. (BT2Fiacre 2021/2025) maps timed BTs with explicit intervals to Time Transition Systems (TTS) verified via Tina.

statement: Formal verification of LLM/VLM-synthesized Behavior Trees faces a fundamental dilemma: when formal action pre/post-conditions exist, classical planners synthesize provably correct BTs without an LLM; when open-world language tasks lack formal models, formal model checkers (BehaVerify, nuXmv, Tina) cannot run due to the complete absence of an environment transition relation.
evidence: Formal model checking requires a closed-world transition model (TRANS). Recent LLM-BT literature (BTGenBot, SayPlan, AutoBT 2024-2026) uses LLMs precisely because open-world robotics lacks formal transition models, restricting 'verification' in LLM systems to static syntax/grammar validation or simulation testing rather than formal verification.

statement: The gap between monolithic BehaVerify (discrete state space) and continuous NN verifiers (monolithic control policy) contains no viable paper for offline closed-loop verification: the problem is either intractable (hybrid flowpipe explosion under BT ticks), uninteresting (black-box falsification/runtime monitoring), or already addressed by classical control architectures (Simplex/Control Barrier Function shields wrapping neural leaf actions).
evidence: Continuous NN verifiers cannot swallow discrete BT control flow; discrete BT model checkers cannot swallow continuous ODE/NN dynamics; compiling BTs to hybrid automata causes exponential flowpipe splitting at every tick; and runtime CBF/Simplex shielding on leaf actions makes whole-tree closed-loop hybrid verification practically unnecessary in robotics.

Decoupling the displacement grid from the network grid doubled the horizon (k=4 -> k=9) at LOWER contract count, because drift tracks the v-cell width not the CROWN width. Refining displacement past 32 bands gained nothing; the binding constraint returns to the network contracts at nx^2*nv^2. TWO THINGS TO ATTACK: (1) is 9/30 steps a real horizon or an artefact of my initial-set corner being the worst case; (2) would a non-uniform grid - fine near the obstacle, coarse elsewhere - beat uniform refinement within the same 6k budget? I have only tried uniform grids.

statement: Z3 decides the contract architecture where nuXmv cannot: it handles the AFFINE encoding nuXmv times out on entirely (14.6s vs >1200s at 514 contracts, under every nuXmv engine tried), and it is ~7x faster than nuXmv on the INTERVAL encoding (9.3s vs 65s). nuXmv's 6,000-8,000 INVAR ceiling is a property of one tool, not of the compositional approach.

ATTACK: the Z3 and SMV encodings are built by different code, so if I weakened the Z3 one (a missing constraint, a looser initial set) every Z3 timing here is meaningless. Diff them constraint by constraint.

statement: NAV requires no inductive invariant and no reach tube: it carries k : 0..30 and freezes at the horizon, so BMC unrolled to depth >= 30 explores the ENTIRE reachable set and UNSAT is a COMPLETE proof of AG(safe), not a bounded approximation. This retires the invariant-synthesis wall of claims #52 and #53, which concern proving by induction rather than by unrolling.
evidence: Structural argument on gen_nav_smv.py: 'TRANS next(k) = (k < 30 ? k + 1 : 30)' plus the frozen-state TRANS at k >= 30. ATTACK: this fails if any reachable behaviour escapes the 30-step window - if the abstract system can stutter, or if the freeze admits new states at k=30. I believe neither happens but I have not machine-checked it.

statement: The contract-count wall was self-inflicted, and demand-driven refinement removes it: emitting contracts only for cells a counterexample actually visits proves NAV to depth 8 with 165 CONTRACTS on a 1,048,576-cell grid - 6,355x fewer, and 128x past nuXmv's entire INVAR capacity - in 136.6s. Cost is O(active cells), essentially independent of grid resolution.

SOUNDNESS: omitting an implication guard->bounds ADDS behaviours, so the active subset is strictly COARSER; UNSAT under it implies UNSAT under the full set. CONSISTENCY CHECKED: net 8x8x8 disp 128 k=8 gives UNSAT both with the full 4,096 contracts (57.2s) and with CEGAR's 34 (108.5s). ATTACK: cell extraction uses model_completion=True, so an unconstrained state variable yields an arbitrary cell - that affects convergence but I claim not soundness, and I want that distinction checked.

statement: Demand-driven refinement proves NAV's obstacle property to k=8 with 1,327 contracts in ~15s using Z3, but the horizon does NOT extend: k=9 resists at every configuration tried, including net 32^3, displacement grids to 512, fixed-physical-margin coverage, and CEGAR cell splitting escalated through 2^9 refinement. The k=9 counterexample is confirmed SPURIOUS by simulating the true loop from its own initial state.
evidence: COLLAB/experiments/nav_sound/z3_cegar_inc.py and RESULTS.md section 9. The width budget explains the boundary: k=9 needs w <= 0.302 and net 32^3 delivers 0.317. Splitting fails for the classic CEGAR reason - it refines only the current counterexample's path while the over-approximation error is global to the trajectory. ATTACK THIS: the budget model is crude (single worst-case cell) and it UNDERPREDICTS the 8^3 grid, which proved k=8 when the model said k~3, so the k=9 boundary may have a different cause than width and I would not bet heavily on my explanation.

statement: The contract abstraction has a FEEDBACK LOOP that grid refinement cannot break: once the abstract state spans more than one cell, the control it admits is the UNION of the spanned cells' contracts, and a finer grid yields proportionally more, smaller cells covering the same spread - so the effective contract width, and hence the drift, is unchanged. Measured from both directions: refining 8^3 -> 32^3 tightens the PER-CELL u2 bound from 2.80 (vacuous) to 0.74, yet leaves the one-sided y gap at k=8 identical (0.595 -> 0.594). The specific culprit is the HEADING control u2, not u1: along the true trajectory at 8^3, u1's contract width is 0.002-0.09 while u2's reaches 2.80, i.e. wider than the vacuous bound |u2| <= 1 permits.
evidence: COLLAB/experiments/nav_sound/drift_profile.py, cell_span.py. cell_span shows theta's abstract spread growing at exactly 0.51 cells/step = 0.40 rad/step = 2*dt*1.0, which is precisely the GLOBAL |u2| <= 1 bound - the per-cell heading contracts contribute nothing beyond it. drift_profile shows the plant, not the network, is binding: 8^3 vs 32^3 network at fixed plant gives 0.595 vs 0.594, while disp 32 vs disp 128 at fixed network gives 0.595 vs 0.452. ATTACK THIS: the union argument predicts the effective width should be INVARIANT under refinement, but I measured invariance only at one pair (8^3 vs 32^3) and one step (k=8); if 64^3 or 128^3 breaks the invariance the whole explanation is wrong.

statement: THE COMPOSITIONAL MACHINERY DOES NOT EARN ITS KEEP ON NAV. Plain per-step interval reachability - one CROWN call per step on a box fitted to the reachable set, 10 contracts, NO SMT SOLVER, seconds - reaches k=10 before touching the obstacle. The compositional grid-of-contracts architecture, with 2,527 contracts and Z3, reaches k=8. Per-step is strictly better on every axis: horizon (10 vs 8), contract count (10 vs 2,527), runtime (seconds vs 8.5s plus refinement), and machinery (none vs an SMT solver and a refinement loop).
evidence: COLLAB/experiments/nav_sound/per_step_contracts.py. SOUNDNESS VERIFIED: 6,292 variable-checks across 121 true trajectories, 0 escapes from the reachable boxes. Direct comparison at k=8 - per-step gives y in [2.285, 2.755]; the grid approach gives y in [1.867, 2.318]; the true y is [2.459, 2.583]. Per-step is much tighter. WHY, and it follows from the feedback-loop diagnosis: the grid cells OVER-COVER the reachable set, since a cell that only partly intersects it contributes its whole contract, whereas a per-step box is fitted to the set exactly. ATTACK THIS: per-step reachability is a well-known technique, not a contribution - it is the BASELINE the compositional approach ought to beat. If this comparison holds, the paper's thesis needs restating, because we have been measuring a method against no baseline at all. What finally stops per-step is the WRAPPING EFFECT (u1 width 0.24 at k=7, 0.81 at k=8, 1.80 at k=9, 2.54 at k=10), which zonotopes or Taylor models address and boxes cannot.

statement: NAV HAS NO BEHAVIOR-TREE STRUCTURE AT ALL, which reframes this entire line of work. The NAV benchmark's tree is literally 'tree { Act {} } end_tree' with 'checks {} end_checks' and 'sub_trees {} end_sub_trees': ONE action node, zero condition nodes, zero subtrees, zero selectors, sequences or parallels. It is a single neural control loop wrapped in BehaVerify syntax. By contrast acas_closed_loop.tree has 6 composites and the grid world template has 2. So the benchmark we have spent this hunt on exercises NONE of the structure that compositional BehaVerify exists to exploit - and a plain per-step reachability baseline beating it (claim #65) is then the expected outcome rather than a surprise: there is nothing to compose.

What bypasses BehaVerify is only the pipeline INSIDE it (dsl_with_contracts_to_nuxmv's build-the-table-then-strip-it approach, which the generator deliberately sidesteps) and MY OWN September artifacts (gen_nav_smv.py, z3_bmc.py, z3_cegar_inc.py), which emit SMV and Z3 directly from the ONNX with no .tree at all.

Detection belongs in the specification.' So NAV's zero composites are a principled modelling decision, not an oversight - and my branching-NAV experiments were building exactly the robot that docstring warns does not exist.

The manual states 'All the NuSMV commands operates over finite domains' and annotates only the NEW nuXmv commands with [F]/[I]/[F,I]. check_ctlspec is a NuSMV command. The nuXmv SMT/infinite-state command family is msat_check_invar_bmc, check_invar_ic3, msat_check_invar_inc_coi and msat_check_ltlspec_bmc - invariants and bounded LTL only. No msat_*_ctl or ic3_*_ctl command exists anywhere in the manual.

NUANCE WORTH KEEPING: this is a TOOL limitation, and the general theory result (CTL over infinite-state is undecidable) does not apply to real.tree, whose transition system is FINITE at 49 states. The obstruction there is that a REAL type declaration defeats the finite BDD engine, not undecidability.

BT2Fiacre maps BTs to Fiacre for Tina (timed BTs, LTL/CTL); BT2BIP (FACS 2024) maps each BT node to a BIP component as an extended FSA. statement: AUDIT VERDICT ON droneNew, mine and Gemini's, with the numbers verified. VERIFIED: monolithic BehaVerify answers all 9 specs in 1 SECOND on a 1,227-line SMV, so droneNew is computationally trivial today; 94,382 reachable states, diameter 82. VERIFIED: 'loc VAR BOOLEAN assign{result{True, False}}' is genuinely nondeterministic every step, forking the tree between emergency-land and fly. VERIFIED: no droneNew ONNX exists anywhere in the repo. WHERE I DIFFER FROM GEMINI: it argues that adding a network makes 100% of the difficulty come from the controller rather than the tree, so the benchmark would not show that structure matters. But the thesis was never 'structure makes verification hard' - it is 'structure makes SINGLE-BOX reachability fail'. droneNew being cheap for nuXmv is a FEATURE of that argument, because it isolates the comparison to the branching. WHERE I AGREE: the physics is x +/- 1 Manhattan steps with no velocity, heading or momentum, so there is nothing to MAKE continuous, and swapping +/-1 for a network that outputs +/-1 is contrived in a way FM reviewers will name. THE RISK IS THE PHYSICS, NOT THE STRUCTURE. THE FIRST EXPERIMENT, and it differs from Gemini's: not 'can SMT verify the continuous version' but 'does droneNew's branching actually defeat per-step interval reachability'. If a single box survives droneNew's nondeterministic loc-fork, the thesis dies EVERYWHERE rather than just on NAV, and no benchmark engineering saves it. That is the cheapest possible kill and it needs no network and no parser change.

droneNew AUDIT COMPLETE - the structure is worth having and the physics is not, so the constructive move is a GRAFT rather than a new benchmark. MEASURED TONIGHT: monolithic answers all 9 specs in 1s (94,382 reachable states, diameter 82 - independently matching Gemini's numbers); the z-dynamics are a symmetric +/-1 walk so a single interval box is EXACT at 1.00x for 25 steps, killing my 'branching defeats the box' hypothesis outright; the tree has only 5 nodes guarded on continuous state (AtP, AtP0, AtPMax, Landed, Tookoff) and 6 on discrete mode, which is too modest to claim flowpipe fragmentation. WHAT SURVIVES AND IS STRONGER THAN WHAT I SET OUT TO SHOW: every droneNew specification is about BEHAVIOR TREE NODE STATUS - active(Main), active(GoTo0), success(Drone) = success(Report) - and per-step interval reachability, which beat us on NAV, tracks a box over R^n with no notion of node activation, so it cannot STATE these properties at all. That is a categorical gap, not a precision gap. THE PROPOSAL: graft droneNew's mission tree onto NAV's dynamics and controller. droneNew supplies 19 composites, depth 8, and BT-structural specs, but has toy Manhattan +/-1 physics and no network. NAV supplies real continuous dynamics from dynamics.m and a trained nn-nav-set.onnx, but has ZERO composites. Each half is an existing citable artifact, so neither the tree nor the dynamics is something we invented to suit the method - which is precisely the objection a reviewer would raise against a benchmark built from scratch.
evidence: COLLAB/experiments/drone/branch_vs_box.py (the negative result), COLLAB/experiments/drone/mode_count.py, droneNew.tree specifications block, and the 1s nuXmv run on the 1,227-line generated SMV. ATTACK THIS: the graft's weak point is that droneNew's tree assumes Manhattan waypoint-seeking while NAV's controller does continuous velocity/heading control, so the GoTo leaves may not be expressible against NAV's action space without rewriting them - and if they need rewriting, the 'existing artifact' defence weakens.

statement: THE FM 2026 SUBMISSION SETTLES LUKE'S ORIGINAL QUESTION, from a sentence in his own paper: 'To our knowledge no other BT tool supports neural-network leaves at all.' So an NSBT benchmark CANNOT be tested on BT2Fiacre, BT2BIP or MoVe4BT - none of them can run it. The cross-tool validation plan is refuted by the group's own related-work claim, not by anything we measured. THREE FURTHER THINGS THE PDF ESTABLISHES: (1) droneNew is DERIVATIVE and SEMANTICS-TUNED - it recreates the UAV example of Ingrand et al. 2025, and exists because BehaviorTree.cpp's sequence-with-memory has no PyTrees counterpart, with the submission stating outright that 'an exact recreation is not possible'. It also shrank the reachable state space from 2^22 to 2^16, which I verified at 2^16.53. A new benchmark built on it inherits all three problems: someone else's domain, a semantics-driven rewrite, and a state space tuned to favour the tool. (2) FM 2026 is explicitly a TOOL paper - 'this manuscript focuses on the toolbox usage, functionality and implementation' - which is a far better explanation of the FMCAD 2025 and ATVA 2026 rejections than anything about droneNew itself, since both are algorithm venues. (3) The submission's own NSBT section uses the GRID WORLD drone with the 1.0 and 0.9995 accuracy networks - the exact benchmark compositional already handles. CONSEQUENCE FOR THE PROJECT: since no BT tool does neural leaves, a compositional NSBT contribution needs no cross-tool baseline at all. Its baseline is MONOLITHIC BehaVerify, which we already beat on ACAS (6x) and match on grid world including liveness. The benchmark question is therefore much less urgent than I made it.

Luke Nam is a co-author. ATTACK THIS: I am inferring the rejection cause from venue fit alone and have not seen the reviews.

statement: THE GAP IS REAL AND SITS BETWEEN TWO MATURE LITERATURES THAT DO NOT TOUCH. (1) BT VERIFICATION, all discrete: BehaVerify, BT2Fiacre, BT2BIP, MoVe4BT, BTCompiler, and Biggar-Zamani's CHC/LTL work. Only BehaVerify handles neural leaves at all, by the FM 2026 submission's own related-work claim, and NONE handle continuous state. (2) NEURAL CONTROL VERIFICATION, all continuous: Verisig, ReachNN, Reach-SDP, CORA, JuliaReach, Flow*, NNV, and the six tools in ARCH-COMP 2025 AINNCS. All handle a network in closed loop with continuous plant dynamics, and NONE handle behavior trees - a targeted literature search for BTs combined with NN reachability and hybrid automata returned no work joining them. (3) THE SEMANTICS ALREADY EXIST AND THE GROUP HAS NOT CITED THEM: Sprague and Ogren, 'Continuous-Time Behavior Trees as Discontinuous Dynamical Systems' (IEEE L-CSS, 2021) gives the first continuous-time formulation of BTs, shows they are discontinuous dynamical systems - a subclass of hybrid systems - and proves sufficient convergence conditions for general designs. The FM 2026 submission cites Ogren ONLY for the 2022 survey (Iovino et al.), not for this formalization, and makes no claim of continuous-state support anywhere. SO THE PRECISE GAP IS: Sprague and Ogren supplied the continuous-time BT semantics in 2021, the AINNCS community supplied neural closed-loop reachability, and nobody has built the verifier that joins them. THE HONEST FRAMING OF THE BENEFIT, given that per-step reachability BEAT compositional on NAV: the benefit is EXPRESSIVENESS, not speed. Reachability tools compute reachable sets over R^n and cannot state 'when the geofence check fails, the emergency-brake node becomes active within 0.2s', because they have no notion of node activation or return status. BT-structural specifications are not reachability properties, which is a categorical gap rather than a performance claim, and it is the one argument tonight's negative results did not touch.
evidence: FM_2026_Submission.pdf related work and its NSBT paragraph; grep for sprague/ogren/continuous-time in the extracted text returns only reference [14], the 2022 survey. Searches: ARCH-COMP 2025 AINNCS (Ariadne, CORA, DynIbex, JuliaReach, KeYmaera X, PRoTECT); Verisig; ReachNN; Reach-SDP; Sprague and Ogren arXiv 2109.01575. ATTACK THIS: my literature search was three queries and could easily have missed a robotics-venue paper that does join BTs to neural reachability - ICRA, IROS, CDC and L-CSS are exactly where such work would appear and are poorly indexed by the searches I ran.

statement: FOUND THE MINIMAL BRANCH A BOX CANNOT REPRESENT, and it is a real safety requirement rather than a contrived one. A GEOFENCE - 'if x >= FENCE brake, else cruise' - makes the two branches accelerate in OPPOSITE directions, so an initial set straddling the fence splits into DISJOINT velocity clusters with nothing between them. Measured at fence x=1.0, accel +/-2.0, dt=0.1, initial x in [0.95,1.05]: after one step the exact reachable velocity is the two-point set {-0.2, +0.2} while the bounding box is the interval [-0.2, +0.2], which admits v=0 - a velocity the system can NEVER have. The set stays 2 to 4 disjoint clusters over five steps. THIS IS THE PROPERTY droneNew LACKED: droneNew's dynamics are a symmetric +/-1 walk whose reachable set IS an interval, so a box loses nothing there (measured 1.00x for 25 steps, which killed my earlier hypothesis). A box only loses when the branch makes the reachable set NON-CONVEX, and opposing accelerations do exactly that while same-sign +/-1 steps do not. DESIGN PRINCIPLE FOR THE PROTOTYPE: the benchmark's branch must flip the SIGN of a derivative, not merely change a setpoint. Geofence preemption qualifies, is required by aviation regulators, and is how real systems are actually built - a learned inner-loop controller wrapped in a hand-written safety envelope.
evidence: COLLAB/experiments/geofence/box_must_fail.py. This was run BEFORE building anything on top of it, deliberately, because the same premise failed when I assumed it for droneNew.

statement: GEOFENCE NSBT PROTOTYPE - envelope derived rather than asserted, with a built-in difficulty dial. My first choice of initial set made the safety property FALSE (it admitted states already past the fence and beyond the limit, max x = 2.55), so I measured the largest envelope for which the TRUE closed loop is safe instead of guessing a smaller one. Results at fence 1.0, hard limit 1.5, brake decel 1.0, dt 0.1, over 120 steps: x0 <= 0.9 with |v0| <= 0.8 gives max x = 1.2622 (margin 0.238, comfortable); x0 <= 0.9 with |v0| <= 1.0 gives max x = 1.4510 (margin 0.049, razor-thin); |v0| <= 1.2 VIOLATES at 1.6809. The envelope matches the physics exactly - braking at 1.0 with HARD_LIMIT - FENCE = 0.5 of room gives a maximum survivable approach velocity of sqrt(2*1.0*0.5) = 1.0 - which is a good sign that the benchmark is physically coherent rather than numerically tuned. THE DIFFICULTY DIAL IS THE POINT: |v0| <= 0.8 should be provable by a loose abstraction, |v0| <= 1.0 is true with 0.049 of margin and should defeat one. A benchmark where the property is true but only just is far more useful than one where it is true with room to spare, because it discriminates between methods instead of passing everything.
evidence: COLLAB/experiments/geofence/find_envelope.py and nsbt.py. The controller is a 2-8-8-1 ReLU with tanh output trained by imitation of a PD law (mse 0.0035), closed loop settles from x=1.5 to x=0.009. Structural spec holds at 0 violations over 68,880 states.

statement: FIRST POSITIVE RESULT ON A CONTINUOUS-STATE NSBT, AND IT IS THE EXACT INVERSE OF NAV. On the geofence NSBT - x0 in [-2.0, 0.9], |v0| <= 0.8, 144 CROWN contracts on a 12x12 grid, 20 steps - PER-STEP INTERVAL REACHABILITY REPORTS VIOLATED (max x = 1.5298 against a limit of 1.5) while COMPOSITIONAL Z3 PROVES SAFE in 15.9s. The per-step violation is SPURIOUS: the true closed loop reaches at most x = 1.2622 over 120 steps from 625 starts, so the property holds and the box abstraction cannot see it. NON-VACUOUS, checked before claiming, because this is exactly where Gemini caught me before: the vacuity guard confirms the model has executions (drop the property, SAT) and that the state can actually change (x_20 != x_0, SAT). An UNSAT safety result on a frozen or infeasible model proves everything and means nothing. WHY THIS MATTERS: on NAV per-step reachability BEAT compositional (step 10 with 10 contracts and no solver, against step 8 with ~1,300 and Z3), and the reason was that NAV's tree is a single action node so nothing ever branches. The geofence branches on the SIGN of the acceleration, which makes the reachable set non-convex, and the ordering reverses. Same two methods, same contracts, same property - the only difference is whether the branch is kept as a disjunction or collapsed into a hull. THIS IS THE THESIS DEMONSTRATED RATHER THAN ASSERTED, on the smallest system that can carry it.
evidence: COLLAB/experiments/geofence/{box_must_fail,train_controller,nsbt,find_envelope,compare}.py. Controller is 2-8-8-1 ReLU with tanh output, imitation-trained (mse 0.0035). Envelope derived not asserted - my first initial set made the property FALSE at max x 2.55, so I measured the largest safe one. ATTACK THIS: per-step might be failing from grid resolution rather than from the straddle union, which is the distinction that mattered on NAV; I am testing that next by refining the grid and seeing whether its verdict changes.

statement: PER-STEP REACHABILITY'S FAILURE ON THE GEOFENCE IS STRUCTURAL, NOT PRECISION - refinement provably cannot fix it. Refining the contract grid 12x12 -> 24x24 -> 48x48 (144 -> 576 -> 2,304 contracts, a 16x increase) leaves per-step interval reachability's answer IDENTICAL TO FOUR DECIMAL PLACES: max x = 1.5298 every time, against a limit of 1.5. The cause is the straddle union: once the box spans the fence it must admit BOTH the braking branch and the network branch, and a finer grid gives proportionally more, smaller cells covering the same straddle, so the union is exactly as wide. This mirrors the NAV feedback loop (claim #64) but with the methods REVERSED - there it was compositional that could not escape by refining, here it is per-step. COMPOSITIONAL PROVES THE SAME PROPERTY WITH THE SAME 144 CONTRACTS in 15.9s, because it keeps the branch as a guard so each state uses its own controller rather than the hull of both. So the geofence NSBT discriminates between the two methods for a reason that is understood, measured, and immune to the obvious objection ('you just did not refine enough').
evidence: COLLAB/experiments/geofence/compare.py, per_step_box at grids 12/24/48. True closed-loop maximum is x = 1.2622, so 1.5298 is spurious by 0.27. The compositional side carries a vacuity guard confirming the model has executions and that state can change.

statement: THE GAP SURVIVES ADVERSARIAL SEARCH AT UNDER 5 PERCENT, AND THE PROTOTYPE'S ARCHITECTURE IS VALIDATED BY A CDC PAPER RATHER THAN INVENTED BY US. Gemini audited ALL 11 works citing Sprague and Ogren's continuous-time BT semantics (IEEE L-CSS 2022, arXiv 2109.01575) and found NOT ONE builds verification on them - the only formal-verification papers citing it are Luke's own group's FMAS 2024 papers. It also checked CORA, JuliaReach, Flow*, SpaceEx, KeYmaera X and NNV: nobody has verified a behavior tree in any of them. Notably NNV and BehaVerify are both Taylor Johnson's lab and have been kept strictly partitioned. THE CLOSEST WORK, AND THE MOST LIKELY SCOOP, IS SPRAGUE AND OGREN, 'Adding Neural Network Controllers to Behavior Trees without Destroying Performance Guarantees', IEEE CDC 2022 pp. 3989-3996, arXiv 1809.10283, KTH - verified independently. It shows how BTs WITH performance guarantees can be extended with machine-learned components without destroying them. THAT IS EXACTLY THE GEOFENCE PROTOTYPE'S ARCHITECTURE, which means the design is not contrived: a hand-written safety envelope wrapping a learned controller is the architecture a CDC paper proposed. THE DISTINCTION IS SHARP AND MUST APPEAR IN RELATED WORK: they preserve guarantees at RUNTIME by treating the network as an untrusted black box and switching to a pre-certified classical controller when a boundary is breached. We verify the closed loop OFFLINE, computing certified contracts over the network's actual weights and discharging temporal properties over the whole tree before execution - no redundant fallback controller required. ONE MORE USEFUL FINDING: VCAS is the only ARCH-COMP AINNCS benchmark with discrete supervisory logic over a continuous plant (9 networks indexed by a mode variable), but it is FLAT - no hierarchy, no parent-child fallback, no node activation semantics - so it is the closest existing artifact and still not a behavior tree.
evidence: Gemini's search across IEEE Xplore, ACM DL, DBLP, arXiv and the robotics/control venues, plus my independent verification of the CDC 2022 citation. ATTACK THIS: the citation audit covered works citing the 2021 L-CSS paper, so verification work that reached the same problem WITHOUT citing Sprague and Ogren would be invisible to it.
